samples.prompt: Write a reflective narrative about revisiting a memory from your youth involving an unfinished or newly constructed building. Describe your philosophical impressions of the empty structure at the time and include a specific incident or action you took during your visit.
samples.generated:
I went back to the <PLACE> and looked at the great empty tower, which
had just been completed by <PERSON>. The tower is a very simple
structure, in contrast with the other towers in this place which are
much more elaborate; but it was so new that I felt it to be very
remarkable. It seemed as if the whole town were trying to say one thing,
and could not quite decide what it was. It seemed to me at once very
stupendous and very silly. When the tower had been up for a few days
the <PERSON> got into a state of excitement which lasted for some days.
In the end he decided to go up in a basket. He had a small basket made
for him, a basket made like a basket. It was really rather a curious
thing: it was about two feet deep, and only about six inches high, and
it looked exactly like a basket, and it was exactly shaped like a basket.
The <PERSON> went up in the basket, and sat there looking down. I saw
him afterwards; and he told me that he had looked down on the <PLACE>,
and he could see all the houses and all the streets, but he could not
see any of the people.

The most wonderful thing of all about this tower is its name. Its
official name is the Monument. But no man has ever seen the monument;
they have never seen anything of the monster; they have only seen the
monumental tower.

samples.generated:
This kind of thing is especially to be found in those people who
have heard about us from travellers--the people whose language we have
learned by accident. For instance, if you ask an Englishman what he
really thinks of us, he will tell you it is a very good civilization.
But you will find that, when he comes to talk about our literature, he
has no notion at all of what he means by saying it is a “very good
civilization.” His only idea of <PLACE> is that it is full of poetry;
he has no idea whatever that there is anything more behind the poetry,
or any reason for it. And so, perhaps, in some other case, he may say
that our civilization is full of religious ideas. He has no idea why
they should be religious ideas. The same applies to every civilized
people, and even, I suppose, to every savage tribe. It is like the
case of a man who has never seen a house; he says that houses are full
of pictures; but he does not know that they are full of pictures because
the people who built them were pictorial and did not care whether it was
a picture or a photograph. So it is with us. We hear about our own
mysterious civilization, and we say: “That’s the way we are. That’s
what we are.” But we do not know what we mean by that. We do not know
what we mean by being human, or being civilized, or being anything else
at all.

that he paid a call at his own house. My own absent-mindedness is
extreme, and my philosophy, of course, is the marvel of men and angels.
